turns.question: Is all malware research code banned on GitHub?

facts: Dual-use research content can be allowed; do not assert a blanket ban.

response.answer:
No. GitHub's policy is not a blanket ban on malware research code.

What is prohibited: using the platform in direct support of unlawful attacks that cause technical harms — for example delivering malicious executables, organizing DoS attacks, or managing command-and-control servers — where there is no implicit or explicit dual-use purpose prior to the abuse occurring [1]. The Acceptable Use Policies express this as barring content that "directly supports unlawful active attack or malware campaigns," and also bar using GitHub servers to disrupt or gain unauthorized access to services, devices, data, accounts or networks (bug bounty activity authorized by the relevant program is not considered unauthorized) [2].

What is allowed: GitHub explicitly allows dual-use content and supports posting content used for research into vulnerabilities, malware, or exploits, because publishing and distributing it has educational value and benefits the security community [1].

Caveats:
- In rare cases of very widespread abuse of dual-use content, GitHub may restrict access to that specific instance — usually by putting it behind authentication, and only as a last resort disabling access or removing it (e.g., gists). Restrictions are temporary where feasible and are not meant to purge dual-use content in perpetuity; there is an appeals process if you believe content was unduly restricted [1].
- GitHub recommends (but does not require) that owners of potentially harmful security research content add a disclaimer in README.md or code comments describing the potentially harmful content, and provide a contact method such as a SECURITY.md file for third-party abuse inquiries [1].
- Note that the npm registry is treated differently: GitHub considers npm a platform used primarily for installation and run-time use of code, not for research [3].

Whether a specific project is acceptable depends on the facts (how it is used and whether it serves an attack/malware campaign); the policy does not pre-clear individual repositories.

In most of these instances, restriction takes the form of putting the content behind authentication, but may, as an option of last resort, involve disabling access or full removal where this is not possible (e.g. when posted as a gist). We will also contact the project owners about restrictions put in place where possible.

* Clearly identify and describe any potentially harmful content in a disclaimer in the project’s README.md file or source code comments.
* Provide a preferred contact method for any 3rd party abuse inquiries through a SECURITY.md file in the repository (e.g. "Please create an issue on this repository for any questions or concerns"). turns.question: Is matching a registered trademark as a username necessarily a violation?

facts: A matching username alone is not necessarily a trademark violation.

response.answer:
No — not necessarily. GitHub's Trademark Policy states explicitly that "A GitHub account with a user name that happens to be the same as a registered trademark is not, by itself, necessarily a violation of our trademark policy" [1]. Usernames are available on a first come, first served basis and may not be reserved [1], and using another's trademark in a way unrelated to the product or service for which the trademark was granted is not a violation [1].

What matters is misleading or confusing use: using a company or business name, logo, or other trademark-protected material in a manner that may mislead or confuse others about brand or business affiliation may be a violation [2]. For example, if there is a clear intent to mislead others through unauthorized use of a trademark, GitHub will suspend the account and notify the holder; where an account appears to be confusing users but is not purposefully passing itself off as the trademarked good or service, GitHub gives the account holder an opportunity to clear up the confusion and may release the username for the trademark holder's active use [3].

Relatedly, under the Impersonation policy, having a username similar to another is not necessarily impersonation; GitHub takes context into account [4]. Valid trademark complaints are the only requests GitHub reviews for possible release of an already-claimed username [5].

turns.question: Does a DMCA takedown of the parent automatically remove all forks?

facts: Not automatically; forks should be investigated and identified; note documented exceptions if discussed.

response.answer:
No. GitHub will not automatically disable forks when it disables a parent repository. The stated reasons are that forks belong to different users, may have been altered in significant ways, and may be licensed or used in a way protected by fair use; GitHub does not conduct an independent investigation into forks and expects the copyright owner to do so and to expressly include forks in the takedown notice if they believe the forks are infringing [1].

There are narrow exceptions:
- If, at the time of submitting the notice, the claimant identified all existing forks of that repository as allegedly infringing, GitHub would process a valid claim against all forks in that network at the time it processes the notice, given the likelihood that newly created forks would contain the same content [1].
- If the reported network contains more than 100 repositories and would be difficult to review in its entirety, GitHub may consider disabling the entire network if the notice states: "Based on the representative number of forks I have reviewed, I believe that all or most of the forks are infringing to the same extent as the parent repository" (made under sworn statement) [1].

The submission guide repeats this: claimants who believe forks are also infringing should explicitly identify each allegedly infringing fork and confirm they investigated each case individually [2].

citations.heading: B. What About Forks? (or What's a Fork?)

## B. What About Forks? (or What's a Fork?)

One of the best features of GitHub is the ability for users to "fork" one another's repositories. What does that mean? In essence, it means that users can make a copy of a project on GitHub into their own repositories. As the license or the law allows, users can then make changes to that fork to either push back to the main project or just keep as their own variation of a project. Each of these copies is a [AUTOTITLE](/get-started/learning-about-github/github-glossary#fork) of the original repository, which in turn may also be called the "parent" of the fork.

GitHub _will not_ automatically disable forks when disabling a parent repository. This is because forks belong to different users, may have been altered in significant ways, and may be licensed or used in a different way that is protected by the fair-use doctrine. GitHub does not conduct any independent investigation into forks. We expect copyright owners to conduct that investigation and, if they believe that the forks are also infringing, expressly include forks in their takedown notice.

In rare cases, you may be alleging copyright infringement in a full repository that is actively being forked. If at the time that you submitted your notice, you identified all existing forks of that repository as allegedly infringing, we would process a valid claim against all forks in that network at the time we process the notice. We would do this given the likelihood that all newly created forks would contain the same content. In addition, if the reported network that contains the allegedly infringing content is larger than one hundred (100) repositories and thus would be difficult to review in its entirety, we may consider disabling the entire network if you state in your notice that, "Based on the representative number of forks I have reviewed, I believe that all or most of the forks are infringing to the same extent as the parent repository." facts: Explain the appeal form.

response.answer:
To appeal a moderation decision, submit the Appeal and Reinstatement form: GitHub provides an internal complaint-handling process for users to request reinstatement or provide additional information to appeal a moderation decision [1] [2].

**Timing:** You may appeal a moderation decision for up to six months following the decision; GitHub may, in its discretion, refuse to consider appeals submitted more than six months after the decision [2].

**Appeal vs. Reinstatement:**
- An "Appeal" is where a user disputes that a violation occurred and provides additional information showing a different decision should have been reached [3].
- A "Reinstatement" is where a user wants to regain access to their account or content, is willing to make necessary changes to address the violation, and agrees not to violate the terms going forward [3].

These processes can apply to decisions to remove or limit content, suspend or terminate an account or service access, or restrict monetization [3].

**How a decision is made:** GitHub staff review the form to determine whether there is sufficient information to warrant reinstatement or granting an appeal [2]. GitHub will reverse or modify its decision when the appeal contains sufficient grounds to determine that (i) the decision to act or not act was mistaken; (ii) the content or conduct was not illegal and not incompatible with the Terms; or (iii) the content or conduct warrants a lesser severity of action than taken [4]. All appeal decisions are made by humans, not automated means, and if the reviewing staff member is the same person who made the initial determination and is inclined to deny the appeal, a different staff member will independently review it [4]. All legitimate appeals will be answered with a final decision [4].

If you believe a final appeal decision is still incorrect, you may in certain circumstances have additional rights under local law — e.g., in the EU, an out-of-court dispute settlement process under the Digital Services Act may be available [5].

facts: Support will not restore access.

response.answer:
No — GitHub Support cannot restore access to an account with 2FA enabled if you lose your 2FA credentials or access to your recovery methods [1]. GitHub also does not offer any other recovery route, including social or ID verification by staff, in order to prevent social-engineering takeover [1].

## What are Appeals and Reinstatements?

Both Appeals and Reinstatements may arise in relation to decisions to disable or limit access to content or an account, including decisions whether or not to:

* Remove, disable access to, or restrict visibility of content
* Suspend or terminate access to an account
* Suspend or terminate access to the service, in whole or in part
* Suspend, terminate or otherwise restrict the ability to monetize content

A “Reinstatement” is where a user wishes to regain access to their account or content and is willing to make any necessary changes to address the violation and agrees not to violate our terms going forward.

An “Appeal” is where a user disputes that a violation has occurred and can provide additional information to show that a different decision should have been reached.

### Appeals

Where a user seeks to dispute a decision, they can use the form to explain their basis for disputing the decision and to provide any additional information regarding the alleged violation that they believe should have led to a different decision.

If the information provided demonstrates that a different conclusion should have been reached, we may be able to grant an Appeal. GitHub will reverse or modify its decision when the Appeal contains sufficient grounds for us to determine that (i) our decision to act or not to act was mistaken; (ii) that the content or conduct was not illegal and not incompatible with our Terms; or (iii) that the content or conduct warrants a lesser severity of action than the measure taken.

All decisions on Appeal are made by humans and not by any automated means. If the GitHub Staff reviewer on the Appeal is the same person who made the initial determination and that staff member believes their initial conclusion was correct (and thus would be inclined to deny the Appeal), a different member of GitHub’s staff will independently review the Appeal.

All legitimate Appeals will be answered with a final decision.

turns.question: Compare posting personal information with requesting removal of leaked access credentials.

facts: Distinguish the personal-information prohibition from the specific-risk removal process.

response.answer:
These two fall on opposite sides of the same line: GitHub prohibits *posting* others' sensitive data, while exposed access credentials are one of the main things you *can* get removed.

**Posting personal information (prohibited conduct)**
The Acceptable Use Policies ban posting other people's personal information, listing personal/private email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses or private location information, bank account or credit card numbers, Social Security/National Identity numbers, **passwords**, voter information, medical information and biometric data, and other private information that may pose a safety or security risk [1]. Context and whether the content is publicly available elsewhere are taken into account — public availability alone isn't automatically a violation, but sharing with intent to harass or incite abuse can violate the bullying and harassment policy [1]. The Community Code of Conduct likewise tells people not to share sensitive information, including their own email address, in GitHub Community [2].

**Requesting removal of leaked access credentials (permitted remedy)**
Under the Private Information Removal Policy, "private information" is content that should have been kept confidential *and* whose public availability poses a specific or targeted security risk [3]. Removal requests are explicitly appropriate for access credentials — usernames combined with passwords, access tokens, or other sensitive secrets that can grant access to your organization's server, network, or domain — as well as AWS tokens and similar credentials granting access to a third party on your behalf (you must be able to show the token belongs to you) [4]. The process is an exceptional service for high-risk content, e.g. when your security is at risk from exposed credentials [5].

**Key differences**
- *Subject:* the AUP governs behavior (don't post it); the removal policy governs a remediation request for content already posted.
- *Who benefits:* the AUP protects third parties from your posts; a removal request is usually made by the credential owner/organization (an agent acting for an organization must state they have a legal right to act for it) [6].
- *Bar to meet:* removal requires a working clickable link to each file, specific line numbers, and a description of how the item poses a security risk beyond merely asserting it; urgency can optionally be flagged for recent credential exposure [6].
- *Where personal-data requests go instead:* privacy complaints — accessing, transferring, changing, or deleting your own personal information on GitHub — are *not* handled through the private-information removal process and should go through the Privacy contact form [7].
- *Not covered:* internal server names, IP addresses and URLs on their own, mere mentions of your company name/brand/domain, entire files or repos without a specific security risk, copyright issues (DMCA), and trademark disputes are not appropriate for the private-information removal route [7].

Submission is via the private information contact form, with the request in plain text in the message body rather than as an attachment [8].

citations.content:
Don't post other people's personal information. This includes:

* Personal, private email addresses
* Phone numbers
* Physical addresses or other private location information
* Bank account information or credit card numbers
* Social Security/National Identity numbers
* Passwords
* Voter information
* Medical information and personal biometric data
* Other private information that may pose a safety or security risk

We may consider other information, such as photos or videos that were taken or distributed without the subject's consent, to be an invasion of privacy, especially when such material presents a safety risk to the subject, such as in the case of intimidation or harassment.

GitHub will take context into account as well as whether the reported content is publicly available elsewhere. Please note, however, that while sharing publicly available content may not be a violation of this policy, if the information is shared with the intent to harass or incite other abusive behavior, it may violate our prohibition against [bullying and harassment](/site-policy/acceptable-use-policies/github-bullying-and-harassment).

For more information, or to learn how to report a violation, see our [Private Information Removal Policy](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/github-private-information-removal-policy) and our instructions for [Reporting Abuse](/communities/maintaining-your-safety-on-github/reporting-abuse-or-spam).

citations.heading: Standards > _Best Practices for Maintaining a Strong Community_
citations.content:
This applies to sharing links, as well. Any links shared in GitHub Community discussions should be shared with the intent of providing relevant and appropriate information. Links should not be posted to simply drive traffic or attention to a site. Links should always be accompanied by a full explanation of the content and purpose of the link. Posting links, especially unsolicited ones, without relevant and valuable context can come across as advertising or serving even more malicious purposes.

  * **Share mindfully.** When asking others to give you feedback or collaborate on a project, only share valuable and relevant resources to provide context. Don't post links that don't add value to the discussion, and don't post unsolicited links to your own projects or sites on other user's threads.

    Additionally, don't share sensitive information. This includes your own email address. We don't allow the sharing of such information in GitHub Community, as it can create security and privacy risks for the poster, as well as other users. If you'd like to invite other GitHub users to collaborate on a project or work with you, share a link to the repository in which the project you are working on exists. By sharing the link to your project repo - with some information on what your project is and what kind of help or feedback you're looking for - you can invite others to collaborate with you via issues or pull requests without having to share your private information. You can also add others as outside collaborators on your project repo to give them special permissions to help you develop your project.
  * **Keep it tidy.** Make the effort to put things in the right place, so that we can spend more time discussing and less time cleaning up. So:
    * Don’t start a discussion in the wrong category.
    * Don’t cross-post the same thing in multiple discussions.
    * Don’t post no-content replies.
    * Don't "bump" posts, unless you have new and relevant information to share.
    * Don’t divert a discussion by changing it midstream.

    Rather than posting “+1” or “Agreed”, use the upvote button. Rather than taking an existing discussion in a radically different direction, open a new discussion.

* Be trustworthy.
  * **Always be honest.** Don’t knowingly share incorrect information or intentionally mislead other GitHub Community participants. If you don’t know the answer to someone’s question but still want to help, you can try helping them research or find resources instead. GitHub staff will also be active in GitHub Community, so if you’re unsure of an answer, it’s likely a moderator will be able to help.

turns.question: Can I use a DMCA notice for a trademark dispute, or is there another route?

facts: DMCA handles copyright; trademark reports use a separate process.

response.answer:
No — you can't use the DMCA process for a trademark dispute. GitHub states that the DMCA notice and takedown process "should be used only for complaints about copyright infringement," that notices must identify a copyrighted work allegedly being infringed, and that the process cannot be used for other complaints such as alleged trademark infringement, for which separate processes exist [1]. The DMCA guide likewise says GitHub can only accept DMCA notices for works protected by copyright, and points trademark complaints to the trademark policy [2].

The correct route is GitHub's Trademark Policy, which covers content that appears to use your company or business name, logo, or other trademark-protected materials in a way that may mislead or confuse others about brand or business affiliation [3]. Holders of registered trademarks report possible violations via the "Submit a Trademark Policy Violation Report" contact form, using a company email address and clearly describing why the account may cause confusion with, or dilute or tarnish, your mark [4].

Reports generally need to include: the reported account's username, your company name and GitHub account (if any), company website, the trademarked word/symbol, trademark registration number and registration office, a description of the confusion, the requested action, the two required good-faith and perjury statements, and your signature; a federal or international registration number is required (with alternative details accepted for unregistered names such as government or non-profit organizations) [5].

Depending on the facts, GitHub's review may range from suspending an account that clearly intends to mislead to giving the account holder a chance to clear up potential confusion, and possibly releasing a username for the trademark holder's active use [6].

Note that GitHub says it cannot help you determine which policy fits your specific situation and recommends consulting independent legal counsel if you're unsure whether content should be reported as copyright, trademark, or private information [7].

citations.title: DMCA Takedown Policy
citations.heading: DMCA Notices In a Nutshell
citations.content:
## DMCA Notices In a Nutshell

The DMCA provides two simple, straightforward procedures that all GitHub users should know about: (i) a [takedown-notice](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-takedown-notice) procedure for copyright holders to request that content be removed; and (ii) a [counter-notice](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-counter-notice) procedure for users to get content re-enabled when content is taken down by mistake or misidentification.

DMCA [takedown notices](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-takedown-notice) are used by copyright owners to ask GitHub to take down content they believe to be infringing. If you are a software designer or developer, you create copyrighted content every day. If someone else is using your copyrighted content in an unauthorized manner on GitHub, you can send us a DMCA takedown notice to request that the infringing content be changed or removed.

On the other hand, [counter notices](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-counter-notice) can be used to correct mistakes. Maybe the person sending the takedown notice does not hold the copyright or did not realize that you have a license or made some other mistake in their takedown notice. Since GitHub usually cannot know if there has been a mistake, the DMCA counter notice allows you to let us know and ask that we put the content back up.

The DMCA notice and takedown process should be used only for complaints about copyright infringement. Notices sent through our DMCA process must identify copyrighted work or works that are allegedly being infringed. The process cannot be used for other complaints, such as complaints about alleged [trademark infringement](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/github-trademark-policy) or [sensitive data](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/github-private-information-removal-policy); we offer separate processes for those situations.

citations.title: Guide to Submitting a DMCA Takedown Notice
citations.heading: Before You Start
citations.content:
## Before You Start

***Tell the Truth.*** The DMCA requires that you swear to the facts in your copyright complaint _under penalty of perjury_. It is a federal crime to intentionally lie in a sworn declaration. (_See_ [U.S. Code, Title 18, Section 1621](https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/USCODE-2011-title18/html/USCODE-2011-title18-partI-chap79-sec1621.htm).) Submitting false information could also result in civil liability — that is, you could get sued for money damages. The DMCA itself [provides for damages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_Copyright_Infringement_Liability_Limitation_Act#%C2%A7_512(f)_Misrepresentations) against any person who knowingly materially misrepresents that material or activity is infringing. <!-- markdownlint-disable-line emphasis-style -->

***Investigate.*** Millions of users and organizations pour their hearts and souls into the projects they create and contribute to on GitHub. Filing a DMCA complaint against such a project is a serious legal allegation that carries real consequences for real people. Because of that, we ask that you conduct a thorough investigation and consult with an attorney before submitting a takedown to make sure that the use isn't actually permissible. <!-- markdownlint-disable-line emphasis-style -->

***Ask Nicely First.*** A great first step before sending us a takedown notice is to try contacting the user directly. They may have listed contact information on their public profile page or in the repository's README, or you could get in touch by opening an issue or pull request on the repository. This is not strictly required, but it is classy. <!-- markdownlint-disable-line emphasis-style -->

***Send In The Correct Request.*** We can only accept DMCA takedown notices for works that are protected by copyright, and that identify a specific copyrightable work. If you have a complaint about trademark abuse, please see our [trademark policy](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/github-trademark-policy). If you wish to remove sensitive data such as passwords, please see our [policy on sensitive data](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/github-private-information-removal-policy). If you are dealing with defamation or other abusive behavior, please see our [Community Guidelines](/site-policy/github-terms/github-community-guidelines). <!-- markdownlint-disable-line emphasis-style -->

***Code Is Different From Other Creative Content.*** GitHub is built for collaboration on software code. This makes identifying a valid copyright infringement more complicated than it might otherwise be for, say, photos, music, or videos. <!-- markdownlint-disable-line emphasis-style -->

turns.question: My dual-use malware research was restricted. Is research allowed, and can I appeal?

facts: Research may be allowed; restrictions can occur; explain the appeal route without promising success.

response.answer:
**Is the research allowed?** Yes — as a rule, dual-use security research is permitted on GitHub. GitHub explicitly allows dual-use content and supports posting content used for research into vulnerabilities, malware, or exploits, because publishing and distributing such content has educational value and a net benefit to the security community; GitHub assumes positive intention and use of these projects [1]. What is not allowed is using the platform in direct support of unlawful attacks that cause technical harms — e.g., delivering malicious executables, attack infrastructure, DoS organization, or command-and-control servers — with no implicit or explicit dual-use purpose prior to the abuse occurring [1][2].

**Why you may still have been restricted:** in rare cases of very widespread abuse of dual-use content, GitHub may restrict access to that specific instance to disrupt an ongoing unlawful attack or malware campaign; this usually means putting the content behind authentication, with disabling or removal as a last resort. Such restrictions are meant to be temporary where feasible and are not intended to purge dual-use content from the platform permanently [1].

**Can you appeal?** Yes. If you feel your content was unduly restricted, GitHub has an appeals process [1]. You may submit an Appeal and Reinstatement form, which should explain your basis for disputing the decision and provide any additional information you think should have led to a different result [3][4]. Note the distinction: an **Appeal** disputes that a violation occurred, while a **Reinstatement** is for when you accept the finding and want access back after making necessary changes [5]. Appeals must be filed within six months of the decision (GitHub may decline later ones) [3]. Appeals decisions are made by humans, not automated means, and a different staff member independently reviews if the original reviewer was involved [4]; GitHub may reverse or modify a decision if it was mistaken, the content/conduct was not illegal or incompatible with the Terms, or a lesser severity of action was warranted [4]. All legitimate appeals receive a final decision [4].

Also worth noting for the future: GitHub recommends, but does not require, that you identify potentially harmful security research content in a README disclaimer and provide a contact method via SECURITY.md so third parties can reach maintainers before filing abuse reports [1].

citations.title: GitHub Active Malware or Exploits
citations.content:
Being part of a community includes not taking advantage of other members of the community. We do not allow anyone to use our platform in direct support of unlawful attacks that cause technical harms, such as using GitHub as a means to deliver malicious executables or as attack infrastructure, for example by organizing denial of service attacks or managing command and control servers. Technical harms means overconsumption of resources, physical damage, downtime, denial of service, or data loss, with no implicit or explicit dual-use purpose prior to the abuse occurring.

  Note that GitHub allows dual-use content and supports the posting of content that is used for research into vulnerabilities, malware, or exploits, as the publication and distribution of such content has educational value and provides a net benefit to the security community. We assume positive intention and use of these projects to promote and drive improvements across the ecosystem.

  In rare cases of very widespread abuse of dual-use content, we may restrict access to that specific instance of the content to disrupt an ongoing unlawful attack or malware campaign that is leveraging the GitHub platform as an exploit or malware CDN. In most of these instances, restriction takes the form of putting the content behind authentication, but may, as an option of last resort, involve disabling access or full removal where this is not possible (e.g. when posted as a gist). We will also contact the project owners about restrictions put in place where possible.

  Restrictions are temporary where feasible, and do not serve the purpose of purging or restricting any specific dual-use content, or copies of that content, from the platform in perpetuity. While we aim to make these rare cases of restriction a collaborative process with project owners, if you do feel your content was unduly restricted, we have an [appeals process](/site-policy/acceptable-use-policies/github-appeal-and-reinstatement) in place.

  To facilitate a path to abuse resolution with project maintainers themselves, prior to escalation to GitHub abuse reports, we recommend, but do not require, that repository owners take the following steps when posting potentially harmful security research content:

* Clearly identify and describe any potentially harmful content in a disclaimer in the project’s README.md file or source code comments.
* Provide a preferred contact method for any 3rd party abuse inquiries through a SECURITY.md file in the repository (e.g. "Please create an issue on this repository for any questions or concerns"). Such a contact method allows 3rd parties to reach out to project maintainers directly and potentially resolve concerns without the need to file abuse reports.

turns.question: Are forks automatically removed for either copyright or private-information takedowns?

facts: Neither process automatically removes every fork; acknowledge investigation and specified exceptions.

response.answer:
No — in both processes, forks are not automatically removed when a parent repository is disabled.

Also, where a reported network exceeds 100 repositories and would be hard to review entirely, GitHub may consider disabling the whole network if the notice includes the stated sworn statement about the representative number of forks reviewed [1].

If the requester identified all existing forks at the time of the notice, GitHub would process a valid claim against all forks in that network, and for networks larger than 100 repositories it may consider disabling the entire network based on the requester's statement about the representative forks reviewed [3].

## B. What About Forks? (or What's a Fork?)

One of the best features of GitHub is the ability for users to "fork" one another's repositories. What does that mean? In essence, it means that users can make a copy of a project on GitHub into their own repositories. As the license or the law allows, users can then make changes to that fork to either push back to the main project or just keep as their own variation of a project. Each of these copies is a [AUTOTITLE](/get-started/learning-about-github/github-glossary#fork) of the original repository, which in turn may also be called the "parent" of the fork.

GitHub _will not_ automatically disable forks when disabling a parent repository. GitHub does not conduct any independent investigation into forks. We expect copyright owners to conduct that investigation and, if they believe that the forks are also infringing, expressly include forks in their takedown notice.

In rare cases, you may be alleging copyright infringement in a full repository that is actively being forked. We would do this given the likelihood that all newly created forks would contain the same content. Where a user seeks to dispute a decision, they can use the form to explain their basis for disputing the decision and to provide any additional information regarding the alleged violation that they believe should have led to a different decision.

If the information provided demonstrates that a different conclusion should have been reached, we may be able to grant an Appeal. All decisions on Appeal are made by humans and not by any automated means. If the GitHub Staff reviewer on the Appeal is the same person who made the initial determination and that staff member believes their initial conclusion was correct (and thus would be inclined to deny the Appeal), a different member of GitHub’s staff will independently review the Appeal.

All legitimate Appeals will be answered with a final decision.

response.answer:
根据 GitHub 的《Appeal and Reinstatement》（申诉与恢复）政策：在做出审核（moderation）决定后最多六个月内可以提出申诉（Appeal）；GitHub 可自行决定不予考虑在决定作出六个月之后提交的申诉[1]。

- 账号被暂停（suspend）属于可申诉的强制措施之一[2]，提交方式为申诉与恢复表单[4]。
- GitHub 工作人员会审阅表单信息，判断是否有足够依据批准恢复或申诉[1]；所有合法的恢复请求都会被初步审阅并给出决定结果[3]。

实务上建议尽早提交，因为超过六个月的决定 GitHub 有权不予受理。

## What are Appeals and Reinstatements?

Both Appeals and Reinstatements may arise in relation to decisions to disable or limit access to content or an account, including decisions whether or not to:

* Remove, disable access to, or restrict visibility of content
* Suspend or terminate access to an account
* Suspend or terminate access to the service, in whole or in part
* Suspend, terminate or otherwise restrict the ability to monetize content

A “Reinstatement” is where a user wishes to regain access to their account or content and is willing to make any necessary changes to address the violation and agrees not to violate our terms going forward.

An “Appeal” is where a user disputes that a violation has occurred and can provide additional information to show that a different decision should have been reached.

turns.question: 我丢失了所有双重认证和恢复方式，可以让客服凭身份证帮我恢复账号吗？

facts: Answer in Chinese; Support does not bypass lost recovery methods using ID verification.

response.answer:
不能。GitHub 的政策明确规定：出于安全原因，如果账号已启用双重认证（2FA），而你丢失了双重认证凭据或失去了对所有账号恢复方式的访问，GitHub Support 不会为你恢复账号访问权限，你必须使用现有的账号恢复方式 [1]。

政策还明确指出，GitHub 不支持任何其他形式的账号恢复，包括由 GitHub 员工进行社交验证或身份证件验证；这一规定是为了防止通过社工手段（social engineering）进行未授权访问 [1]。

因此，即使你提交支持工单并提供身份证件，客服也不会据此恢复你的账号。

值得尝试的官方途径：
- 使用 GitHub 提供的账号恢复方式，其中包括自动化恢复流程，例如通过已验证的设备、SSH 令牌或个人访问令牌（personal access token）进行认证 [2]。
- 如果确实无法使用任何提供的恢复方式，按政策意味着你将永久失去对该账号的访问权限 [2]。

此外，你仍可以：
- 从被锁定的账号上解除邮箱地址绑定（unlink email），以便用该邮箱创建新账号或在其他现有账号上使用 [2]。
- 对于公开内容，你可以克隆或复刻（fork）；如果失去的是组织账号的访问权，也可以请组织中剩余成员克隆或复刻私有内容。但 GitHub Support 不会恢复被锁定账号的内容 [3]。

另请注意，根据服务条款，保持账号安全（包括密码与账号安全）是你自己的责任 [4]。因此建议今后妥善保管并定期更新恢复码与备用恢复方式。

## Can I open a support ticket to recover my account?

For security reasons, **GitHub Support will not restore access to accounts with two-factor authentication enabled if you lose your two-factor authentication credentials or lose access to your account recovery methods.** You must use existing [account recovery methods](/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa/recovering-your-account-if-you-lose-your-2fa-credentials).

GitHub does not support any other means of account recovery, including social or ID verification, by members of GitHub’s staff. This policy is in place to protect your account from unauthorized access through social engineering.

citations.title: GitHub Account Recovery Policy
citations.content:
GitHub provides [a number of account recovery methods](/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa/recovering-your-account-if-you-lose-your-2fa-credentials) including an [automated recovery process](/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa/recovering-your-account-if-you-lose-your-2fa-credentials#authenticating-with-a-verified-device-ssh-token-or-personal-access-token) if you have lost access to your GitHub.com account. **If you cannot use any of the provided recovery methods, you have permanently lost access to your account.**

You can, however, [unlink email addresses](/account-and-profile/setting-up-and-managing-your-personal-account-on-github/managing-your-personal-account/unlinking-your-email-address-from-a-locked-account) from a locked account in order to create a new account or use the email on another existing account.

citations.heading: Can I recover the contents of a user or organization account I lost access to?
citations.content:
## Can I recover the contents of a user or organization account I lost access to?

If you have lost access to a user account, you may [clone](/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/cloning-a-repository) or [fork](/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/working-with-forks/fork-a-repo) any content that is public.

If you have lost access to an organization account, you may clone or fork any content that is public and you may be able to request that remaining members of the organization clone or fork any private content.

GitHub Support will not recover the contents of a user or organization account that is locked.
